name: Tomato
summary: The pantry workhorse: sauce, salsa, canned tomatoes and fresh eating. Needs heat, sun and support.
problems:
Early blight shows as brown rings on lower leaves; pick them off and mulch to stop soil splashing up. Blossom end rot (a dark, sunken bottom) comes from uneven watering. Hornworms are big green caterpillars; pick them off by hand.

Fruit stops setting when nights stay above about 24 °C (75 °F) or days pass 32 °C (90 °F), so in hot places plant early or again for fall.
greenhouse_notes: Grows well in a greenhouse in spring and fall. Open vents on hot days, since flowers drop when it's too hot, and gently shake the flowering stems to help pollination.
notes: Paste types (like Roma) have less water and make thicker sauce with less cooking. Determinate varieties ripen in a few weeks, handy for canning; indeterminate ones keep producing until frost.

name: Sweet pepper
summary: Bell and other sweet peppers for fresh eating, roasting, freezing and pickling. Slow to start, so begin early.
problems: Seeds sprout slowly in cool soil; use a heat mat. Flowers drop in very hot or cold spells. Sunscald makes pale, papery patches on fruit; leafy plants shade their own fruit.
greenhouse_notes: Peppers love greenhouse warmth and can keep producing into winter in a heated one.
notes: Green peppers are simply unripe; leave them on the plant to turn red, yellow or orange for sweeter flavor and more vitamins.

name: Hot pepper
summary: Jalapeños, serranos, poblanos, cayenne and more. Easy in heat and very productive in a pot.
problems: Same as sweet peppers: slow cool-soil germination, flower drop in extreme heat. Wear gloves when picking and cutting the hottest kinds.
greenhouse_notes: Thrives in a greenhouse; plants can be kept over winter in a warm one and will produce earlier the next year.
notes: Dry thin-walled peppers like cayenne by stringing them up in a warm, airy place. Ripe red jalapeños smoked dry become chipotles.

name: Eggplant
summary: Loves real heat. Glossy fruit for roasting, grilling and stews.
problems: Flea beetles chew tiny holes in young leaves; cover plants with row cover until they flower. Cold nights stall growth, so don't rush planting out.
greenhouse_notes: A greenhouse gives eggplant the steady warmth it wants, especially where summers are short.
notes: Pick while the skin is shiny. Dull skin means seeds are getting hard and the flesh bitter.

name: Potato
summary: A storage staple grown from seed potatoes, not seeds. Easy, and fun to dig.
problems: Potatoes turn green and bitter in light; keep them covered with soil or mulch. Colorado potato beetles and their orange larvae eat leaves; pick them off. Don't plant where tomatoes or potatoes grew last year.
notes: Buy certified seed potatoes; grocery potatoes may carry disease or be treated to stop sprouting. Grow bags work well and make harvest easy.

name: Sweet potato
summary: Grown from slips (sprouted shoots). Loves heat, shrugs off drought once settled, and stores for months.
problems: Cold soil stunts slips; wait until it's truly warm. Voles and deer like them. Harvest before soil drops below about 13 °C (55 °F).
notes: The 'start indoors' dates here are for growing your own slips from a sweet potato set half in water or damp soil. Bought slips go straight out at transplant time. The leaves are edible too.

name: Onion
summary: A kitchen staple that stores for months. Picking the right day-length type for where you live matters most.
problems: Onions hate weeds; keep them clear. Bulbs split or bolt after cold snaps or uneven watering. Stop watering when tops start to fall over.
notes: Onions bulb when days reach a certain length. In the south (roughly below 35° latitude, like Texas and much of Mexico) grow short-day onions, planted in late winter. Farther north grow intermediate or long-day types. Buying transplants or sets is easier than seed for beginners.

name: Garlic
summary: Planted in fall, harvested in early summer. Almost no work, and a year's supply fits in a small bed.
problems: Waterlogged soil rots cloves; plant in well-drained beds. Keep weeds down in spring.
notes: Softneck garlic suits mild winters and stores longest; hardneck suits cold winters and makes edible scapes in spring. Plant cloves from a garden supplier, not the grocery store. Save your biggest bulbs to plant next fall.

name: Carrot
summary: Sweetest from cool weather. Sown straight in the bed in loose, stone-free soil.
problems: Seeds are slow and must stay moist for up to three weeks; a board laid over the row helps. Forked roots come from rocky or compacted soil. Green shoulders come from light; cover the tops with soil.
notes: Short or round varieties suit heavy soil and pots. A light frost makes carrots sweeter, and they keep in the ground into winter where it doesn't freeze hard.

name: Beet
summary: Two crops in one: roots and tender greens. Quick, easy and good pickled.
problems: Each beet 'seed' is a cluster that grows several plants, so thinning matters. Woody roots come from heat or dry soil.
notes: Eat the thinnings as baby greens. Roots are tender at golf-ball to tennis-ball size.

name: Radish
summary: The fastest crop in the garden, ready in about a month. Great for beginners and for filling gaps.
problems: Heat makes radishes hot, pithy and quick to flower; grow them in spring and fall. Flea beetles nibble leaves.
notes: Sow a short row every week or two for a steady supply. Winter radishes like daikon are sown in late summer and store well.

name: Lettuce
summary: Salad all spring and fall. Loose-leaf types can be picked again and again.
problems: Heat makes lettuce bolt (send up a flower stalk) and turn bitter; give it afternoon shade in warm weather. Slugs love it; trap them under boards.
greenhouse_notes: An unheated greenhouse grows lettuce through most of the winter.
notes: Seeds need light to sprout, so barely cover them. Sow a little every two weeks instead of all at once.

name: Spinach
summary: A true cool-season green, sweetest in cold weather. Freezes well for winter cooking.
problems: Bolts quickly once days get long and warm. Seeds sprout poorly in warm soil, so sow in cool weather.
greenhouse_notes: Survives winter in an unheated greenhouse or under row cover in most places.
notes: Pick outer leaves to keep plants going, or cut the whole plant at once.

name: Kale
summary: Tough, productive greens you pick leaf by leaf for months. Frost makes it sweeter.
problems: Cabbage worms (green caterpillars) and aphids are the usual pests; row cover keeps the white moths off. Summer heat makes leaves tough.
greenhouse_notes: Keeps producing through winter in an unheated greenhouse.
notes: Harvest the lowest leaves first and leave the top growing. Goats and chickens enjoy the extras.

name: Cabbage
summary: Firm heads for slaw, cooking and sauerkraut. Grow it in the cool ends of the year.
problems: Same pests as kale. Heads split after heavy rain or watering when they're mature; harvest promptly.
notes: Fall-grown cabbage is usually the best. Store whole heads in a cool, damp place for weeks.

name: Broccoli
summary: Big central heads, then side shoots for weeks after. Freezes well.
problems: Heat makes heads loose and flowery; cut before the yellow flowers open. Same pests as kale.
notes: After cutting the main head, leave the plant: smaller side shoots keep coming.

name: Green bean
summary: Easy, fast and generous. Bush beans need no support; pole beans climb and keep producing longer.
problems: Seeds rot in cold, wet soil; wait until it's warm. Mexican bean beetles eat leaves from underneath. Don't handle wet plants, which spreads disease.
notes: Pick every few days while pods are slim and the seeds inside are small. Let some pods dry on the plant to save seed or to cook as dry beans.

name: Pea
summary: One of the first crops of spring. Shelling, snap and snow peas all like it cool.
problems: Heat ends the harvest; plant as early as the soil can be worked. Powdery mildew whitens leaves late in the season.
notes: Most varieties need a trellis or netting about 1 to 1.5 m (3 to 5 ft) tall. Pea shoots make good microgreens too.

name: Cucumber
summary: Fast summer vines for salads and pickles. Grow them up a trellis to save space.
problems: Cucumber beetles (yellow with black stripes or spots) spread wilt; cover young plants until they flower. Bitter fruit comes from heat or dry soil. Powdery mildew is common late in summer.
greenhouse_notes: Choose greenhouse or 'parthenocarpic' varieties, which set fruit without bees.
notes: Pick pickling cucumbers small and often; one missed cucumber left to yellow slows the whole vine.

name: Zucchini
summary: Summer squash that grows almost too well. Two plants feed a family.
problems: Squash vine borers make plants suddenly wilt; look for sawdust-like frass at the stem base. Squash bugs gather under leaves; scrape off the bronze egg clusters. Powdery mildew is common and mostly cosmetic late in the season.
notes: Pick at 15 to 20 cm (6 to 8 in); they get big fast. The flowers are edible.

name: Winter squash
summary: Butternut, acorn, kabocha and more. Grows all summer and stores into spring.
problems: Same pests as zucchini. Butternut types resist vine borers better than most.
notes: Vines need lots of room; let them run along a fence or into a path. Cure and store as on the harvest guide; whole squash keep for months.

name: Pumpkin
summary: For pies, soups and storage. Big vines, big harvest.
problems: Same pests as zucchini. Fruit sitting on wet soil can rot; set it on a board or straw.
notes: Small 'pie' or 'sugar' pumpkins taste better than carving types. Pumpkin purée shouldn't be home-canned; can cubes or freeze the purée.

name: Sweet corn
summary: Plant in blocks, not single rows, so the wind can pollinate it. Best eaten within hours of picking.
problems: Poor pollination leaves gappy ears; plant at least four short rows side by side. Corn earworms enter the tip of the ear; just cut off the damaged end. Raccoons know when it's ripe.
notes: Keep different sweet corn types (or popcorn) apart or planted at different times, since cross-pollination spoils the sweetness.

name: Okra
summary: A Southern favorite that thrives in the heat other crops can't stand. Pretty hibiscus-like flowers.
problems: Seeds sprout poorly in cool soil; soak them overnight and sow in warm soil. Pods turn woody in just a day or two.
notes: Pick pods at 5 to 10 cm (2 to 4 in) every other day. Wear gloves and long sleeves; many plants have prickly leaves.

name: Cowpea (black-eyed pea)
summary: A heat-loving bean eaten fresh or dried. Feeds the soil and needs little care.
problems: Aphids cluster on new growth; a strong spray of water knocks them off. Stinkbugs can mark the seeds.
notes: Pick pods green to shell fresh, or leave them to dry on the plant for storage. The vines make good goat feed after harvest.
